idiom_name: small domestic interface + struct with methods over net/http or database/sql
implementation_notes: Go dissolves the class structure: declare the domestic interface in the consuming package, implement it with a struct that holds the foreign client (*http.Client, *sql.DB, a gRPC generated client) plus the base address, and provide a New... constructor so the zero value never reaches production code. Errors are values, so the foreign error model is translated by wrapping with context (fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)) or by mapping into sentinel/typed errors (ErrNotFound) rather than by exceptions; status codes must be translated explicitly because net/http reports 4xx/5xx as a successful round trip. Injecting the *http.Client or *sql.DB keeps tests local: httptest.Server, a custom http.RoundTripper or a stub implementing the domestic interface all substitute for the connection.
pitfalls: The zero value of the struct is unusable: with the foreign client left nil the first call panics, so the constructor must be the only way to build a gateway (or New must return an error).
Forgetting to thread the context (or to set a timeout on the http.Client) lets a gateway call hang a goroutine forever with no way for the caller to cancel it.
net/http never turns a 404/500 into an error: a gateway that ignores resp.StatusCode makes every caller repeat the translation, and usually gets it wrong.
sql.Rows and sql.Stmt must be closed (defer rows.Close()) or the database/sql pool leaks connections until the process stalls.
